body.p: After , (the backtracking matcher) and (perf-6: compiling is now under 5 % of a regex-heavy workload; matching is the rest). Measured (release, x86_64 Xeon 2.1 GHz): 200,000 calls of matches("abc_def ghi " || ., "\w+\s\w+\s\d+") take 0.80 s, and 0.71 s with explicit ranges [a-z_]+ [a-z]+ [0-9]+, against 0.12 s for the same loop with contains: about 3 microseconds a match of a 15-character string, whatever the character classes.

item.p: Mechanism: profile first (callgrind on tests/bench/regex-reuse.xq and a new matching benchmark), then general mechanisms of the one regex engine for the hot spots. Candidates to confirm or reject with numbers: the matcher created and released on every call ( kept matchers per call; a matcher could live with its cache entry while no call uses it); the setup and the backtrack stack of each match; a literal prefix or a required first character to skip start positions; ASCII fast paths for class tests in src/regex_unicode.c (generated: change tools/generate-regex-tables.py and regenerate, never edit it). Errors, the regex step limit and step counts stay as before.
Owns: src/regex.c, src/regex_internal.h, src/regex_unicode.c, tools/generate-regex-tables.py, src/function_library_regex.c, tests/regex_test.c, tests/bench/regex-*.xq.

Done when: each change measured before and after (instructions and seconds) in a D-record and the commit messages; the QT4 XP40 and XQ40 regex sets and the XT40 regex sets unchanged case by case; , the memory limits and honest step counts kept. Done 2026-10-28 (): ASCII member sets and an ASCII category table, a start filter, idle matchers in the regex cache, character repetitions; 200,000 matches 0.382 to 0.197 s (366.9 to 200.3 x 10^6 instructions at 20,000), regex-match.xq 1.069 to 0.652 s, regex-reuse.xq 0.250 to 0.146 s; QT4 and XT40 regex sets unchanged case by case.
